body.hook: You can recognize a Van Gogh from across a room by the swirling brushstrokes, or a Kenojuak Ashevak print by its bold, balanced shapes. That recognizable quality is style. After three years of art, you're starting to have one too.

study.title: What Makes It Mine?
study.question: What makes my art recognizably mine?
study.passage:
Studio steps (written for this lesson):
1. Look: Compare two artworks by Vincent van Gogh (such as The Starry Night, 1889) and two by Kenojuak Ashevak. List what makes each artist recognizable: subjects, colours, lines, materials, mood.
2. Gather (15 minutes): Lay out at least eight of your artworks from Grades 7–9 (or photos of them).
3. Find patterns (15 minutes): What subjects do you return to? Which media do you choose? What colours? Do you prefer realism, abstraction or something in between? Which works are you proudest of and why?
4. Influences (10 minutes): Name two artists (from class, books, games, comics, animation or social media) whose work you admire. What have you borrowed from them?
5. Style statement (10 minutes): Write three sentences beginning: "My work often...", "I am influenced by...", "Next I want to try..."

body.hook: When you walk into a gallery, there's usually a small card beside each artwork or a statement on the wall. Those few sentences can change how you see the work. An artist statement is your chance to tell viewers what to look for.

study.title: In My Words
study.question: How do I explain my art clearly to others?
study.passage:
Artist statement guide (written for this lesson):
Length: 100–150 words. Written in first person.
Paragraph structure:
1. What: what the work (or body of work) is about, in one clear sentence. "My series explores how my street changes from morning to night."
2. How: materials and process, and why you chose them. "I combined watercolour with collage from local bus maps to show movement through the neighbourhood."
3. Why: what you hope viewers think or feel, or what you learned. "I want viewers to notice ordinary places they usually rush past."
Avoid: "I just made it because I like it"; long lists of every step; vague words like "interesting" or "cool"; over-complicated jargon.
Sample weak statement (written for this lesson): "This is my art. I used lots of stuff. It is about life and it's really cool."
Revise it using the guide, then write your own for your strongest work or series.

body.objective: Students will be able to curate and present a portfolio.

body.hook: A gallery curator doesn't hang every painting an artist ever made. They choose, order and arrange works so the show tells a story. Today you curate your own work into a portfolio and exhibition that shows who you are as an artist.

study.title: Curate Yourself
study.question: How do I choose and present work that shows who I am as an artist?
study.passage:
Portfolio guide (written for this lesson):
1. Select (15 minutes): From your Grades 7–9 work, choose 6 to 8 pieces. Include: your strongest work, a work that shows growth (an early piece beside a later one), a work showing a skill (perspective, portrait, printmaking), a series or mixed-media piece, and one that shows your personal style.
2. Order: Decide how to tell your story: by time (showing growth), by theme, or from strongest to most experimental.
3. Labels: Write a label for each work: Title, Medium, Size (cm), Year.
4. Statement: Attach your artist statement from last lesson.
5. Exhibition (one lesson): Display portfolios as a class exhibition. Visitors leave one comment card per portfolio.
6. Reflection (10 minutes): Write about how you've grown since Grade 7 and what you want to explore in high school art.
